catalog_quote: Accent in the Japanese language is called a pitch accent controlling the 'high-and-low' correlation recognized between moras (in the Tsugaru dialect, such correlation is recognized between syllables). ... Many morphemes have either one takis or no takis and some have more than one takis in the underlying forms. ... According to the place of the "fall of pitch", three accent patterns are recognized. They are named "the initial accented pattern", "the middle accented pattern" and "the final accented pattern". The pattern which has no "fall of pitch" like [?ame], [?amega], etc., is named "the atonic pattern". ... In the word /hana/'flower' /na/ has a higher pitch than /ha/ as [hana], but it is a different pattern from [hana] 'nose'. sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.49: kernel-less type in Aomori = ○○[○ (final rise), types 1-3 Tsugaru [○○]○, ○[○]○, ○○[○]]; p.62-63: 'the loanword accent system, like native words, is based on Pn = n+1 oppositions (one more than the mora count)', with no kernel-less type in 1-2 mora words and word-final kernel a minority; 4-mora loans have 5 contrasts, main types 3, 2, 1. Confirms lexical pitch-accent class; refines the record's secondary loanword rule (Kobayashi's 'penultimate syllable' generalization) with mora-based type distributions for Hirosaki/Goshogawara/Tsugaru-shi speakers.
sources.locator: p.49 (notation: ascending kernel, tonal shapes for Tsugaru vs Iwate per type 0-3), pp.53-63 (sec.2), p.62-63 (2.6 summary)

sources.quote: p.103-104: accent is given as presence/position of an 'ascending kernel' (昇り核, [) counted from word-initial, 0 = kernel-less type; 'all points except Kazamaura (Shimokita) are clearly ascending-kernel dialects'; Hirosaki tonal shapes illustrated (売[ルトキ]], [取ル]トキ); accent type is lexical per verb (e.g. Goshogawara mugu 1 vs mugu 0). No mention of stress/intensity.
